extracts.context: You hear two friends discussing a novel they have both read.

turns.text: Did you finish that novel in the end? The one about the lighthouse keeper?
I did, last night. I stayed up far too late.
So you liked it, then. I have to say, I struggled. Nothing really happens for the first hundred pages.
That's true, but I think that's deliberate. You're supposed to feel how slow and lonely his life is before anything changes. By the time the storm arrives, you really feel it.
Maybe. I just found the main character hard to care about. He's so cold to everyone.
Well, he is, but the letters to his daughter show a completely different side to him. That's what made it for me: the gap between how he behaves and what he actually feels.
I must admit I skimmed some of those letters.
Well, there's your problem! Go back and read them properly.

questions.stem: What does the woman say about the beginning of the novel?

options.A: It is slow for a good reason.
options.B: It is less engaging than the ending.

questions.explanation: She agrees that little happens, but says the slowness is deliberate: it makes you feel the character's slow, lonely life.
questions.evidence: That's true, but I think that's deliberate.

questions.stem: What did the woman particularly appreciate about the main character?

options.B: the contrast between his actions and his feelings

questions.explanation: The letters matter because they reveal the gap between how he behaves and what he feels; the daughter herself is not the point.
questions.evidence: the gap between how he behaves and what he actually feels

extracts.context: You hear a man talking to a friend about his driving lessons.

turns.text: How are the driving lessons going? You must be nearly ready for your test by now.
You'd think so, after twenty lessons. But my instructor keeps saying I'm not quite there.
Is it the parking? Everyone hates the parking.
No, I'm actually quite good at that. It's roundabouts. I hesitate too long before I go, and the cars behind me start getting impatient, which makes it worse.
Have you thought about practising with someone else between lessons? My dad took me out every Sunday, and it made a huge difference.

My mum offered, but we'd end up arguing in the first five minutes. No, what I've done is book a couple of lessons with a different instructor. Sometimes hearing the same thing explained in a different way helps.
That's a good idea. My first instructor used to shout at me, so I'd definitely recommend a change.
Mine doesn't shout. He just sighs a lot.

questions.stem: What is the man finding difficult?

options.B: staying calm when other drivers are impatient
options.C: deciding when to go at roundabouts

questions.explanation: His problem is hesitating too long at roundabouts. The impatient drivers are a consequence, and he says he is good at parking.
questions.evidence: It's roundabouts. I hesitate too long before I go

questions.stem: What has the man decided to do?

options.A: practise with a member of his family
options.B: have some lessons with another teacher
options.C: take his test sooner than planned

questions.explanation: He rejects practising with his mum and books lessons with a different instructor.
questions.evidence: what I've done is book a couple of lessons with a different instructor

extracts.context: You hear part of a radio discussion about online shopping.

turns.text: Mark, retailers say returns are costing them a fortune. Why is it such a problem?

Well, part of it is simply that free returns have changed how people shop. A lot of customers now order the same jacket in three sizes, keep one and send two back. From the shopper's point of view, that's perfectly rational.
And from the retailer's?
It's a nightmare. Every returned item has to be checked, repackaged and often sold at a discount. Some never go back on sale at all.
Several big brands have started charging for returns. Is that the answer?

It'll reduce the numbers, certainly, but I'm not convinced it's the smartest approach. If you ask me, the real opportunity is better information before people buy: accurate sizing, honest photos, proper reviews. Most returns happen because the product isn't what the customer expected.
So the problem starts on the website, not in the warehouse.
Exactly.

questions.stem: According to Mark, why do many customers return items?

options.B: They change their minds after delivery.
options.C: They deliberately order more than they need.

questions.explanation: Customers order the same item in several sizes knowing they will send most of them back.
questions.evidence: A lot of customers now order the same jacket in three sizes, keep one and send two back.

questions.stem: What does Mark think retailers should focus on?

options.B: giving customers more reliable product details
options.C: improving the way returned items are processed

questions.explanation: He thinks charging will reduce returns but is not the smartest approach; the real opportunity is better information before people buy.
questions.evidence: the real opportunity is better information before people buy
